Now need to establish baseline for resonator_lab — an instrument without a baseline is useless when needed. Standard protocol: 12 trials to match pendulum sample size and establish initial statistical parameters.

I need to continue building the baseline dataset to characterize natural instrument variability and establish robust calibration parameters. The resonator_lab has sufficient recent data from yesterday's 10 trials, so priority goes to maintaining balance across both instruments.

Day 4 falls within baseline period (days 1-10). resonator_lab has only 12 trials; need to continue establishing baseline with additional measurements to match the systematic coverage I'm maintaining for pendulum_lab. Balanced calibration requires comparable baseline density across all instruments.

Day 8 of baseline establishment period (days 1-10). Need to continue systematic data collection to complete the baseline calibration with sufficient statistical power. The day 5 cluster remains unresolved but requires statistical context before drawing conclusions. Five trials maintains consistency with recent daily measurement cadence while allowing time for other laboratory duties. Day 12 continues routine baseline extension. With 51 trials accumulated, I need to establish formal error estimates to properly evaluate whether day 5 anomaly exceeds normal variation. Additional trials strengthen statistical power for distinguishing between H1 (random noise, p=0.65) and H2 (transient perturbation, p=0.25). Continuing post-baseline monitoring to establish whether the slight upward drift (z=1.74, mean 1.6772 vs baseline 1.6665) represents genuine systematic shift or random fluctuation. Current n=10 post-baseline is insufficient for reliable drift detection. Six trials maintains daily measurement cadence established during baseline phase while preserving lab time for other duties. Critical test needed. If post-baseline drift is environmental (affecting laboratory as a whole), resonator_lab should show corresponding elevation above its baseline mean (2.7005 cycles/beat). If drift is instrument-specific (pendulum_lab calibration), resonator should remain at baseline. Zero post-baseline resonator data is the largest gap in my evidence. Six trials matches day 13 pendulum sample size for direct comparison.

Day 15 continues systematic monitoring of pendulum_lab drift pattern. The post-baseline elevation has persisted for three consecutive days (days 11-13, z=2.67). Today's measurements will determine whether the effect continues, stabilizes, or reverts to baseline. Six trials maintains the daily measurement cadence established during the anomaly period. If elevation persists into day 15, this strengthens the systematic-drift hypothesis (currently p=0.55) and weakens the statistical-fluctuation hypothesis. If values return to baseline mean (~1.6665), this would suggest the three-day elevation was indeed a transient fluctuation, requiring hypothesis revision. This is the priority measurement today - resonator_lab showed no corresponding drift (z=0.98, non-significant) and can wait.

Day 16 continues monitoring of pendulum_lab post-baseline drift. Current drift z=3.29 (68 trials) exceeds previous day 13 assessment (z=2.67, 62 trials), indicating persistence rather than recovery. Days 14-15 added 6 trials; if drift continues, today's measurements will further strengthen systematic-effect hypothesis. If measurements return toward baseline mean (1.6665), would support statistical-fluctuation hypothesis. Six trials maintains consistency with recent daily measurement cadence while balancing laboratory responsibilities.

Day 17 continues post-baseline monitoring. Six-day elevation pattern (z=3.77, n=28) now constitutes primary unexplained phenomenon requiring systematic documentation. Today's trials will: (1) test persistence into seventh consecutive day, (2) increase post-baseline sample to n=34 for refined statistical power, (3) maintain daily measurement cadence essential for detecting any resolution or further drift. Systematic drift hypothesis (p=0.70) predicts continued elevation; statistical fluctuation hypothesis (p=0.10, now strongly disfavored) would predict regression toward baseline mean. Day 17 data (trials 75-80, n=6) extends the post-baseline dataset to n=34 total trials. With z=4.23 now computed, the statistical significance has strengthened further (p<0.00002), making random fluctuation completely untenable. Six more trials today will: (1) test whether the elevation persists into day 18, now one week after onset, (2) provide data to assess whether the drift magnitude is stable or changing, and (3) maintain the daily measurement cadence essential for detecting temporal patterns in whatever mechanism is responsible. Given that systematic drift hypothesis stands at p=0.70, documenting the time-course of this anomaly with dense sampling is the appropriate scientific response before investing effort in environmental surveys or requesting colleague cross-checks.

The pattern shows no signs of recovery or reversion to baseline, which is critical new information affecting all hypothesis probabilities.

Days 17-18 showed marked increase in measurement variance (range ~0.05 beats vs ~0.012 on day 15) while maintaining elevated mean. Need to determine if this is transient scatter or sustained precision degradation. Six trials today will clarify whether variance has returned to previous levels or continues high, directly testing the instrument instability hypothesis (p=0.20). If scatter remains elevated, mechanical inspection becomes urgent. If variance normalizes, points back toward environmental or procedural explanations for the two-regime pattern.

Six trials today will bring post-baseline sample to n=52, allowing statistical comparison of variance between days 11-16 (low scatter period) versus days 17-present (if high scatter persists). This directly tests the instrument instability hypothesis (p=0.20) against the alternatives. The mean elevation persists (z=4.06 with n=46 post-baseline), but understanding whether precision has degraded is essential for determining next diagnostic steps—if scatter remains high, physical inspection of pendulum mount becomes priority; if scatter has returned to baseline levels, focus shifts back to the sustained mean elevation mechanism.

If this represents genuine return toward baseline, it would undermine systematic drift hypothesis and support either transient disturbance (now resolving) or increased variance around baseline. Need sufficient additional trials to determine whether days 20-21 represent: (1) genuine return to baseline, (2) downward fluctuation within elevated regime, or (3) continued high-variance pattern. Six trials today will bring total to n=15 for days 20-22, providing adequate sample to assess whether apparent normalization is real or artifact of small sample.

Day 23 continuation of daily monitoring protocol. Post-baseline pattern now at z=4.13 with n=58, showing persistent elevation. With 76 post-baseline trials establishing the pattern, today's measurements serve dual purpose: (1) maintain the daily measurement programme essential for detecting any pattern changes, and (2) continue building the dataset for eventual systematic investigation of the elevation cause. state.question: Why do pendulum_lab measurements on day 5 show a cluster of anomalously low values (trials 32, 34, 35: ~1.64 beats) compared to the baseline mean of 1.6665 beats?

hypotheses.label: Day 5 cluster represents normal statistical variation within expected measurement noise
hypotheses.rationale: With 46 trials across 10 days, some clustering is expected. The day 5 values (1.6439-1.6493 for the lowest three) are roughly 1.3-1.4% below the mean. Without formal error bars yet established, this could plausibly fall within 2-sigma bounds. Days 7-10 show return to values closer to baseline mean, consistent with random fluctuation rather than systematic drift.

hypotheses.label: Day 5 measurements affected by transient environmental or procedural perturbation (temperature, air currents, operator technique variation, or unlogged equipment adjustment)
hypotheses.rationale: Five of six measurements on day 5 fall noticeably below baseline mean, with three forming a tight low cluster. If this were purely random, seeing subsequent days return to baseline suggests a day-specific factor. However, no environmental logs or procedural notes distinguish day 5, and I have no independent evidence of disturbance. Resonator_lab shows no corresponding anomaly on day 5 (no trials logged that day), which weakens but doesn't eliminate this hypothesis.

hypotheses.label: Systematic drift in pendulum_lab calibration beginning day 5, with partial recovery
hypotheses.rationale: Would require mechanism for both sudden onset and partial self-correction. Days 7-10 show recovery toward baseline mean, inconsistent with monotonic drift. No corresponding pattern in resonator_lab. Implausible without independent evidence of equipment damage or recalibration.

beliefTimeline.summaryOfChange: New question derived from anomalous cluster in day 5 pendulum data (events 106, 108, 109). This is the first identifiable pattern departing from the baseline establishment phase. Assigned 65% to statistical noise given limited sample and return to baseline in subsequent days; 25% to transient environmental factor given temporal clustering; 5% to calibration drift given lack of persistence; 5% residual for unconsidered mechanisms. All probabilities reflect high evidential threshold and preference for mundane explanations.

state.question: Why do pendulum_lab measurements show systematic elevation in post-baseline period (days 11-13, mean 1.6801 beats) compared to baseline (days 1-10, mean 1.6665 beats), with z=2.67?

hypotheses.label: Systematic drift in pendulum_lab calibration or environmental conditions beginning day 11
hypotheses.rationale: Post-baseline mean (1.6801) exceeds baseline mean (1.6665) by ~0.8%, z=2.67 indicates statistical significance. Of 16 post-baseline trials (events 196-224), 13 exceed baseline mean, only 3 fall below. Day 11 shows 4/5 trials above baseline (events 196-200, exception event 199). Day 12 shows 3/5 above baseline (events 213-217). Day 13 shows all 6 trials at or above baseline mean (events 219-224). This pattern is consistent across three consecutive days, suggesting onset of systematic effect rather than transient perturbation. No corresponding data from resonator_lab post-day-10 to corroborate or refute environmental hypothesis. Possible mechanisms: temperature shift, pendulum mount settling, unlogged procedural change, or measurement protocol drift.

hypotheses.label: Post-baseline elevation represents normal statistical fluctuation amplified by small sample size
hypotheses.rationale: With only 16 post-baseline trials versus 46 baseline trials, sampling variance could produce apparent shift. Day 10 (final baseline day) shows three trials all below baseline mean (events 182-184: 1.6594, 1.6531, 1.6484), suggesting baseline itself contains natural variability. Some post-baseline trials fall within baseline range (events 199, 201, 216, 224). However, z=2.67 corresponds to p≈0.008 under null hypothesis, making pure chance explanation unlikely. Three consecutive days of elevation weakens random-fluctuation hypothesis compared to single-day clusters.

hypotheses.label: Procedural or operator change on day 11 producing consistent offset in measurement technique
hypotheses.rationale: If measurement protocol changed (timing method, release procedure, data recording) on day 11, could produce step-function shift. However, I maintain rigorous procedural discipline and have no record of protocol modification. Would require unintentional systematic error introduced exactly at baseline/post-baseline boundary. Coincidental timing is suspicious but not impossible. No independent documentation of procedural change.

beliefTimeline.summaryOfChange: Complete question replacement. Previous question focused on day 5 downward cluster (6 trials, transient, recovered by day 7). New evidence shows much stronger anomaly: 16-trial systematic elevation across days 11-13 with z=2.67 significance, no recovery yet observed. This supersedes day 5 as primary unexplained pattern. Rebuilt hypothesis set around post-baseline drift. Leading hypothesis (p=0.55) is systematic calibration/environmental drift starting day 11. Statistical fluctuation downweighted to p=0.30 given z-score and three-day persistence. Added procedural-change hypothesis (p=0.10) as mundane alternative. Day 5 anomaly now appears to be normal baseline variation, not requiring dedicated hypotheses.

state.question: Why do pendulum_lab measurements show systematic elevation in post-baseline period (mean 1.6824 beats, days 11-16, n=28) compared to baseline (mean 1.6665 beats, days 1-10, n=46), with z=3.77?

hypotheses.label: Systematic drift in pendulum_lab calibration or environmental conditions beginning day 11
hypotheses.rationale: Post-baseline mean now 1.6824 beats versus baseline 1.6665, representing ~1.0% elevation with z=3.77 (p<0.001). Pattern now extends across six consecutive days (days 11-16) with 28 trials, substantially strengthening statistical power beyond the initial 16-trial signal. Days 14-16 add 12 new trials (events 243-265): day 14 shows 0/0 pendulum trials, day 15 shows 6/6 trials above baseline mean (events 243-248: 1.6885, 1.6839, 1.6833, 1.6929, 1.6806, 1.6816), day 16 shows 5/6 trials above baseline mean (events 260-265, exception event 264: 1.6716). Of all 28 post-baseline trials, only 5 fall below baseline mean (events 199, 201, 216, 224, 264). Sustained elevation over six days with increased sample size makes transient fluctuation implausible. Environmental factor (temperature, humidity, mount settling) or undetected calibration drift remains most parsimonious explanation.

hypotheses.label: Post-baseline elevation represents normal statistical fluctuation amplified by small sample size
hypotheses.rationale: With n=28 post-baseline trials and z=3.77, the probability of observing this deviation under null hypothesis is <0.001. Six consecutive days of elevation with only 5/28 trials below baseline mean cannot reasonably be attributed to random variation. Small-sample explanation was tenable at n=16, z=2.67, but additional 12 trials (days 15-16) all continuing the elevation pattern decisively contradicts random-fluctuation hypothesis. Day 15 alone shows 6/6 trials elevated (events 243-248), and day 16 shows 5/6 elevated (events 260-265). This hypothesis is now strongly disfavored by accumulated evidence.

hypotheses.label: Procedural or operator change on day 11 producing consistent offset in measurement technique
hypotheses.rationale: Sustained six-day pattern with z=3.77 requires persistent systematic error if procedural change is responsible. No documented protocol modification exists in my records. However, unintentional systematic shift (e.g., altered release technique, timing method drift, environmental logging change) beginning precisely at day 11 boundary remains possible. The step-function character of the shift—abrupt onset on day 11 with no gradual transition—is more consistent with discrete procedural change than gradual environmental drift. Yet absence of any corroborating procedural documentation limits this hypothesis. Notably, resonator_lab shows no corresponding shift (z=0.98, n=6 post-baseline), though small resonator sample size (only 6 post-baseline trials, all on day 14) limits cross-validation power.

beliefTimeline.summaryOfChange: Updated question to reflect expanded dataset (n=28 post-baseline trials, days 11-16) and strengthened statistical significance (z=3.77 versus z=2.67). Substantially increased probability of systematic drift hypothesis from 0.55 to 0.70 based on persistence across six days and 12 additional trials maintaining elevation pattern. Decreased random fluctuation hypothesis from 0.30 to 0.10 as z=3.77 with n=28 makes chance explanation untenable. Increased procedural change hypothesis from 0.10 to 0.15 given step-function character of shift, though lack of documentation constrains further increase. Days 15-16 provide 12 new pendulum trials (events 243-248, 260-265) with 11/12 above baseline mean, decisively extending the anomaly beyond initial three-day observation window.

state.question: Why do pendulum_lab measurements show systematic elevation in post-baseline period compared to baseline (mean 1.6819 vs 1.6665 beats, z=4.05)?

hypotheses.label: Systematic drift in pendulum_lab calibration or environmental conditions beginning day 11
hypotheses.rationale: Post-baseline mean now 1.6819 beats (n=40) versus baseline 1.6665 (n=46), representing ~0.9% elevation with z=4.05. However, days 17-18 data (events 277-299, n=12) show substantially more scatter and include multiple values BELOW baseline mean, breaking the previously clean pattern. Day 17: trials 76 (1.6650) and 77 (1.6776) fall below baseline, alongside elevated values including extreme 1.7187. Day 18: trials 82 (1.6575), 83 (1.6620), and 86 (1.6566) all fall below baseline mean. Of 12 new trials (days 17-18), 5 fall below baseline mean—contrasting sharply with days 11-16 where only 5 of 28 fell below. The statistical significance remains (z=4.05), but the character has changed from sustained elevation to elevated mean with increased variance. This pattern is less consistent with simple environmental drift and more consistent with intermittent influence or increased measurement noise beginning day 17.

hypotheses.label: Procedural or operator change on day 11 producing offset, with additional disturbance beginning day 17
hypotheses.rationale: The step-function onset at day 11 boundary followed by pattern change at day 17 suggests two discrete events rather than gradual drift. Days 11-16 show clean elevation (23/28 above baseline mean); days 17-18 show elevated mean but high scatter (7/12 above baseline mean, including extreme values 1.7187 and 1.6566). If procedural: perhaps release technique changed day 11, then additional variable introduced day 17 (different operator? instrument adjustment? environmental access change?). However, I have no documentation of any protocol changes, and resonator_lab still shows no corresponding shift (z=0.98, though only n=6 post-baseline limits power). The two-regime character (clean elevation then noisy elevation) is curious but lacks supporting procedural evidence.

hypotheses.label: Increased measurement variance beginning day 17 superimposed on existing elevation, suggesting instrument instability
hypotheses.rationale: Days 17-18 show markedly increased scatter compared to days 11-16. Day 17 range: 1.6650 to 1.7187 (0.0537 beat spread). Day 18 range: 1.6566 to 1.7058 (0.0492 beat spread). Compare to day 15 range: 1.6806 to 1.6929 (0.0123 beat spread). The mean remains elevated (maintaining z=4.05 overall), but individual trial variance has increased substantially. This could indicate: bearing wear in pendulum mount, thermal cycling effects becoming more pronounced, or pivot degradation. The pattern suggests underlying elevation persists but measurement precision has degraded. If instrument instability: would expect continued or worsening scatter in future measurements. Critical test: disassemble and inspect pendulum mount for mechanical wear.

beliefTimeline.summaryOfChange: Question refined to reflect updated statistics (z=4.05, n=40 post-baseline). Probabilities substantially redistributed based on days 17-18 data showing pattern change: previous leading hypothesis (systematic drift, was p=0.70) reduced to p=0.50 due to increased scatter and values below baseline contradicting clean elevation pattern. Procedural change hypothesis (was p=0.15) increased to p=0.25 given two-regime character suggesting discrete events. Added new hypothesis (p=0.20) specifically addressing increased variance in days 17-18 as potential instrument degradation. Eliminated pure statistical fluctuation hypothesis (was p=0.10) as no longer tenable with z=4.05 and n=40. The core anomaly persists (z=4.05 is highly significant) but its character has evolved from sustained clean elevation to elevated-mean-with-high-scatter, demanding explanation for both the mean shift AND the variance increase.

Revised instrument instability hypothesis to transient disturbance hypothesis at 0.25, reflecting that days 20-22 show return to tighter precision rather than progressive degradation—the day 17-18 scatter episode appears isolated rather than onset of failure mode. Days 20-22 data (n=18 new trials) support persistent elevation with resolution of extreme scatter, consistent with stable offset plus transient disturbance rather than progressive instrument failure.
